mcqs.question: A gas station problem has total gas less than total cost across the whole circuit. What can you conclude?
options: You must simulate every starting point individually to find out if a solution exists
A solution might still exist depending on the order of stations
No valid starting point exists, regardless of where you begin, since the total gas physically can't cover the total distance
There are exactly two valid starting points
mcqs.explanation: Total gas below total cost means no starting point can possibly complete the loop, because the total shortfall exists regardless of where the journey begins — checking this sum up front avoids needing to test any starting point at all when it fails.

mcqs.question: If the tank goes negative at station j starting from candidate station i, why is it safe to skip every station strictly between i and j as a candidate start too?
options: Because those stations always have less gas than station i
It isn't safe in general — each station between i and j must still be tested individually
Because the array must be re-sorted before continuing

Any station k strictly between i and j starts with an empty tank, which is a worse position than the surplus already built up by the time the run from i reached k — if that surplus still went negative by j, starting fresh at k would fail at least as fast
mcqs.explanation: Starting at k means beginning with zero surplus, while the run from i had already accumulated some surplus (possibly negative, but never worse) by the time it reached k. If that accumulated position still couldn't survive to j, an even worse starting position (zero) at k certainly can't either.

mcqs.question: Why is testing every candidate starting station by fully simulating the loop from scratch (O(n²)) considered wasteful here?
options: It produces a different, less accurate answer than the greedy approach
It only works for circular arrays, not linear ones
It ignores the reset rule's insight that one failed simulation already rules out an entire range of other candidates, not just the one tested
It requires sorting the gas and cost arrays first, which the greedy approach avoids
mcqs.explanation: The O(n²) approach gives the same correct answer, just slower — it re-derives information the single-pass reset rule already captures for free, since a single failed attempt eliminates a whole contiguous block of candidates rather than just the one tested.

mcqs.question: What's a key structural difference between Jump Game's running quantity and Gas Station's running quantity?
options: Jump Game's frontier only ever grows and failure ends the whole search; Gas Station's tank balance can go negative, which only eliminates the current candidate range and lets the scan continue with a new one
Gas Station's quantity only ever grows, like Jump Game's
Jump Game allows resets while Gas Station does not
There is no meaningful difference — both algorithms behave identically
mcqs.explanation: Jump Game's frontier is monotone non-decreasing, and running out of reach ends the problem entirely. Gas Station's tank can legitimately go negative, but that failure only rules out a contiguous range of candidate starts — the algorithm resets and keeps scanning rather than terminating.

mcqs.question: Does the single-pass gas station algorithm need explicit modulo-based circular indexing to wrap the scan back to index 0?
options: Yes, without wraparound the answer is always off by one station
Yes, circular problems always require modulo arithmetic to be correct
No — the reset rule and the total-surplus feasibility check together guarantee the final answer is correct using only a single linear pass, with no need to simulate the actual circular wraparound
It depends on whether the gas and cost arrays are the same length
mcqs.explanation: The algorithm's correctness comes from the reset rule and the feasibility check, both of which work correctly over a single linear scan — no explicit circular wraparound simulation is structurally required, even though the underlying problem is framed as a circular route.
